topics.title: Rectangular Cartesian Coordinates in 2 Dimensions
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: draw and label the Cartesian plane. (k, s)
read and plot points on the Cartesian plane/coordinate grid. (k, s)
complete shapes on a coordinate grid. (k, u, s)
choose and uses appropriate scale for a bi-variate data set. (u, s, v/a)

body.text: The Cartesian plane is formed by two number lines crossing at right angles at a point called the origin, (0, 0). The horizontal line is the x-axis and the vertical line is the y-axis. Every point on the plane is described by an ordered pair (x, y), where x tells how far to move along the x-axis and y tells how far to move along the y-axis.

To plot the point (3, 2): start at the origin, move 3 units right along the x-axis, then 2 units up parallel to the y-axis. To plot (-4, 1): move 4 units left, then 1 unit up. A negative x moves left, a negative y moves down.

Shapes can be completed on a coordinate grid using symmetry and known properties. A square has three vertices at (2, 1), (6, 1) and (6, 5). Since all sides of a square are equal and meet at right angles, the fourth vertex must be directly above (2, 1) at the same height as (6, 5), giving (2, 5).

When plotting real data — for example the height and age of several learners — the scale on each axis should be chosen so the data fills most of the grid without being cramped or spread too thin. If ages range from 11 to 16, a scale where each square represents 1 year suits the x-axis; if heights range from 100 cm to 180 cm, each square representing 10 cm suits the y-axis better than 1 cm, which would make the graph far too tall.
